text: Time to put this whole chapter together. Here's a real T-SQL query: a CTE using TOP 5 to grab the five most recent orders, then a SELECT that builds a summary string using plus-sign concatenation and CONVERT with style 101 to format the date. Three pieces here don't translate literally into MySQL: TOP, plus, and that CONVERT style code.

First decision: TOP becomes LIMIT, but it moves. T-SQL's TOP 5 sits right after SELECT. MySQL's LIMIT 5 goes at the very end of the query, after ORDER BY. Not just a renamed keyword — a real structural move.

Second and third decisions, together: MySQL's plus sign is arithmetic only, so string concatenation needs CONCAT instead — CONCAT, order hash, cast order id as char, on, and date format. And that date format call replaces T-SQL's numeric style code entirely, using percent-m, percent-d, percent-Y style tokens instead of the number 101.

Put all three decisions together and here's the fully translated MySQL query — same CTE structure, LIMIT 5 moved to the end, CONCAT in place of plus, DATE_FORMAT in place of CONVERT's style code. Notice the WITH clause itself needed zero changes — that's standard SQL you already covered back in Chapter Four.

That's the real pattern you'll keep seeing across every dialect in this course: most of a query translates untouched. The actual work is spotting the small number of vendor-specific pieces — a row-limiting clause, a concatenation operator, a date-formatting convention — and knowing exactly what each one becomes.

That wraps up MySQL. Next, Chapter Eight: PostgreSQL, starting with PL/pgSQL versus T-SQL — a procedural language modeled more closely on Oracle's PL/SQL than on anything you've seen in T-SQL so far. See you there.
